query: FeCoNi is an fcc alloy with high saturation magnetization and a low coercive field. Earlier studies examined the high-entropy alloys FeCoNiPd and FeCoNiPt, but both exhibited soft ferromagnetism. A qualifying high-entropy alloy must have an almost equiatomic multicomponent composition and configurational entropy of at least 1.0R. Subject to these constraints, what single intervention could produce a FeCoNi-based high-entropy alloy with greater coercivity than the prior derivatives? Present one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the outcome relative to an appropriate FeCoNi-based baseline, defines the conditions over which it should apply, cites supporting observations from earlier work, and proposes a discriminating experiment with an explicit falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: A rapid thermal annealing (RTA) treatment with a tailored, fast cooling rate applied to an equiatomic FeCoNi alloy (without additional noble metals) will induce nanoscale chemical ordering or subtle phase segregation within the fcc matrix, thereby breaking local cubic symmetry. This structure will provide additional domain wall pinning centers and enhance magnetocrystalline anisotropy, resulting in a higher coercive field than that observed in previous FeCoNiPd and FeCoNiPt soft magnetic derivatives.
generation.material_initial_state: Nearly equiatomic, disordered fcc FeCoNi-based high-entropy alloy with high saturation magnetization and low coercivity (soft ferromagnetism)
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled rapid thermal annealing process with a fast cooling rate
generation.conditions: Ambient room temperature magnetic testing; RTA parameters must be optimized to induce nanoscale chemical ordering while retaining the high configurational entropy (≥1.0R) and predominantly fcc structure
generation.structural_mediator: Induced nanoscale chemical ordering/subtle phase segregation within the fcc matrix, leading to local symmetry breaking and the creation of pinning centers
generation.mechanism: Rapid thermal annealing facilitates local atomic rearrangements that create chemical order or nanoscale precipitates without a complete phase transformation. This results in local strain and reduced symmetry that enhances magnetocrystalline anisotropy and provides more effective domain wall pinning, thereby increasing coercivity
generation.predicted_outcome: An increase in the coercive field relative to the baseline FeCoNi-based HEA (e.g., FeCoNiPd and FeCoNiPt) while maintaining high saturation magnetization
generation.baseline: FeCoNi-based high-entropy alloys processed by conventional methods (or with additions such as Pd or Pt) that result in a uniformly disordered fcc structure and soft magnetic behavior
generation.boundary: The effect is expected to hold as long as the equiatomic composition and requisite high configurational entropy are maintained, and the fcc (or comparable high entropy intermetallic) structure is preserved. Extreme deviations in RTA parameters that lead to uncontrolled grain growth or prolific formation of a fully ordered intermetallic phase might nullify the beneficial impact on coercivity
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of the coercivity enhancement is uncertain and will depend on the precise control of the RTA temperature and cooling parameters; there is also a risk that overly aggressive annealing may induce unwanted phase transformations or excessively large grain growth, which could counteract the intended effect

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of equiatomic FeCoNi samples. Process one set using the tailored RTA procedure with a rapid cooling rate and the other set by conventional slow cooling. Characterize both sets using microstructural imaging (HAADF-STEM and SAED) to detect nanoscale ordering or segregation. Measure their magnetic hysteresis loops to determine coercivity and saturation magnetization.
measurements: Grain size and evidence of local ordering (via STEM/SAED)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the RTA-treated samples do not exhibit a statistically significant increase in coercivity (e.g., at least a 2-fold increase) compared to conventionally cooled samples or if the expected nanoscale chemical ordering is absent, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractThe vast high entropy alloy (HEA) composition space is promising for discovery of new material phases with unique properties. This study explores the potential to achieve rare‐earth‐free high magnetic anisotropy materials in single‐phase HEA thin films. Thin films of FeCoNiMnCu sputtered on thermally oxidized Si/SiO2 substrates at room temperature are magnetically soft, with a coercivity on the order of 10 Oe. After post‐deposition rapid thermal annealing (RTA), the films exhibit a single face‐centered‐cubic phase, with an almost 40‐fold increase in coercivity. Inclusion of 50 at.% Pt in the film leads to ordering of a single L10 high entropy intermetallic phase after RTA, along with high magnetic anisotropy and 3 orders of magnitude coercivity increase. These results demonstrate a promising HEA approach to achieve high magnetic anisotropy materials using RTA.Keywords: high entropy alloy, magnetic anisotropy, rapid thermal annealing High entropy alloy (HEA) thin films are explored to achieve high magnetic anisotropy phases. Certain HEA compositions may exhibit long‐range chemical order through the emergence of multiple sublattices, analogous to high entropy ceramics,[  ] leading to so‐called “high entropy intermetallic” (HEI) compounds.[  ] Previously, transition metal alloys with high anisotropy, such as the L10 phases of FePt and FePd have been achieved by annealing of equiatomic solid solution pre‐cursors.[  ] In the case of metastable high anisotropy phases such as L10 FeNi, unconventional annealing techniques have been employed.[  ] In particular, rapid thermal annealing (RTA) of transition metal alloy films on Si/SiO2 is an effective means of inducing high anisotropy phase formation in solid solution precursors, in part due to the substrate‐induced strain.[  ] In this study, we experimentally demonstrate two thin film HEAs with large coercivity and magnetic anisotropy achieved by RTA. We show that RTA treatment of equiatomic FeCoNiMnCu thin films leads to ≈40‐fold increase in coercivity. By introduction of 50 at.% Pt, we realize an L10 HEI phase of (FeCoNiMnCu)Pt with perpendicular magnetic anisotropy resulting from a reduced lattice symmetry and strong spin‐orbit coupling. decision.trend: Early work on FeCoNi‐based high entropy alloys sought to modify intrinsic magnetic properties by changing the composition, for example by adding noble metals (Pd, Pt) to the nearly equiatomic FeCoNi baseline. Although these interventions retained a high saturation magnetization, they did not introduce sufficient magnetocrystalline anisotropy or effective domain wall pinning, so the materials remained soft. Later studies using further compositional modifications – such as the addition of Sn in FeCoNi(CuAl) systems – adjusted phase balances (e.g., FCC plus some BCC) and nanoscale precipitate features, but still did not yield a marked increase in coercivity. A growing trend is the exploration of processing routes that tailor microstructure (e.g. ordering or phase separation) to boost coercivity without deviating from the equiatomic high-entropy constraint.
decision.unsolved: The central remaining challenge is to enhance the intrinsic coercivity of a FeCoNi-based high entropy alloy while keeping an almost equiatomic, high configurational entropy composition. Prior compositional changes alone have not induced sufficient anisotropy or domain wall pinning, leaving the mechanism to produce a hard magnetic variant unresolved.
decision.lever: Apply a controlled rapid thermal annealing (RTA) procedure with a tailored cooling rate to induce nanoscale chemical ordering or a subtle phase segregation within the fcc matrix.
decision.why: Recent observations in related high entropy thin films have shown that post-deposition thermal treatments can induce ordering (e.g., L10 formation) which dramatically increases magnetic anisotropy and coercivity. Using RTA as a single processing intervention directly leverages these findings to create additional domain wall pinning sites and enhance magnetocrystalline anisotropy, thereby addressing the low coercivity issue without altering the equiatomic composition.
